item.title: El-Sayed’s campaign test: Can he win over Black and Jewish voters?
item.dc:creator: Yonat Shimron, Ulaa Kuziez
item.description: DETROIT (RNS) — El-Sayed’s identity as a Muslim and an Arab American is a factor among key constituents in the Democratic Party: Black and Jewish voters.
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

DETROIT (RNS) — During a town hall meeting last week at the Shrine of the Black Madonna, U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged the tensions between the city’s Black residents and its Arab Americans — a tension rooted in economic inequities, race and class.

If elected the first Muslim U.S. senator on Nov. 3, El-Sayed said, he will work to heal the rifts between the two groups. 

Then he made his plea: “I also ask that I am judged by the content of my character, not the color of my skin,” he said at the Sept. 14 event, echoing the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech and winning instant applause from some 100 people seated at tables in the church’s fellowship hall. 

The church, associated with the Civil Rights Movement and affiliated with the United Church of Christ, is one of several Black congregations El-Sayed has visited. He hosted his first campaign launch rally on May 3 at Detroit’s Historic King Solomon Baptist Church.

Detroit, where 75% of 650,000 residents are African-American, is the Blackest city in America. El-Sayed can’t win a Senate seat without strong Black voter turnout. Church town halls, like this one, could make the difference in what is turning out to be a very tight race against the Republican candidate, former congressman Mike Rogers. October surveys show El-Sayed with a small lead, generally between 1 to 3 percentage points. 

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed stressed that he understands the plight of Black Americans and will advocate on their behalf. He highlighted his campaign slogans — “money out of politics” and “Medicare for all.”

The question is whether he can overcome skepticism from this and other religious and ethnic groups.

Black and Jewish voters in and around Detroit both aligned behind Haley Stevens, El-Sayed’s challenger, in the August primaries. He lost in Detroit by 28 percentage points. Now he must win over these two key Democratic constituencies.  On Saturday, Barack Obama is scheduled to stump for him in Detroit. This past week, Sen. Raphael Warnock spoke from the pulpit of a Black church in Flint Michigan, church, saying, “We stand with our brother. Are you with me? We stand with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed.”

RELATED: As Texas Gov. Abbott targets Muslim groups, his PAC receives millions from Muslim oil exec

El Sayed is running at a time of rising Islamophobia. There have been 255 Muslim Americans in elected office in the U.S., according to a new report by the Center for Security, Race and Rights at Rutgers Law School. But despite those historic electoral gains, Muslim Americans running for office consistently face “disproportionate political fearmongering and scapegoating,” the report found. There has never been a Muslim elected as a U.S. Senator.

President Trump has repeatedly slurred him as “Mohammed El-Sayed.” Rogers has tried to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamist movement whose militant offshoots such as Hamas have engaged in armed conflict or terrorism. 

At another town hall meeting recently, a Republican operative heckled El-Sayed, asking: “Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?”

After responding, “Sure. Yeah, absolutely,” El-Sayed then pivoted to questioning the underlying implication — that he had dual loyalties to the U.S. and the Islamist movement. 

He received a warmer welcome at the Shrine of the Black Madonna. Kandia Milton, associate pastor at the church and also chair of a political action group, Black Slate Inc., said the group supports El-Sayed because he “had established some street credibility within our community.”

“He’s not new to us,” Milton said, referring to the doctor-turned-politician’s years of work as director of Detroit’s Health Department and later the Wayne County Department of Health, Human & Veterans Services.

Still, tensions between Black and Arab Americans have existed for decades. After Arab and Chaldean entrepreneurs stepped in to buy up neighborhood gas stations and liquor stores in Detroit, Black customers complained they put up bulletproof glass in some stores and treated them disrespectfully. They also abandoned the city for the suburbs, taking their profits with them rather than investing it in Black neighborhoods.

“A lot of Detroiters just don’t trust Arab Americans because they do business here, but they don’t live here,” said Al Williams, president of the African American Leadership Institute in Detroit.

Just last month, a mob of about 70 people who appeared to be mostly of Arab descent verbally ambushed an injured Black woman whose car was hit by another driver. They shouted anti-Black and sexist slurs at her, according to reports in the Detroit Free Press.

Michigan has never elected a Black candidate to the U.S. Senate, and some Black voters might begrudge an Arab-American Senate candidate getting there first, Al Williams said. 

Charles Williams, pastor of the Historic King Solomon Baptist Church and the Michigan chair of the National Action Network, a civil rights organization led by the Rev. Al Sharpton, agreed that turnout among Black voters will be key for El-Sayed.

“The concern is the small number of folks that say, ‘You know what? I just can’t do it. I’m not gonna do it,’ as well as the small number of folks who’re just gonna say, ‘This time I’m going in another direction,’” Charles Williams said. “It is going to be a tight race, and it is a big challenge that the campaign is gonna have to work to overcome.”   

But it’s not just El-Sayed’s identity as a Muslim and an Arab-American that draws suspicion. It’s also his progressive political positions. In March, after a Lebanese-born man crashed his car into Temple Israel outside Detroit, El-Sayed remarked that “hurt people hurt people.” (The attacker, who lost family members in an Israeli airstrike, died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.)

Many Michigan Jews were offended by the comment, which they viewed as justifying or excusing the attacker’s actions. In August, El-Sayed apologized, saying, “I made a mistake.”

But for many Jews, the damage had been done. At a time of rising antisemitism across the U.S., many of the Jews who make up about 1.4% of Michigan’s population, or about 130,000, say they fear El-Sayed.

Some Michigan Jews are also uncomfortable with El Sayed’s views on Israel. He opposes unconditional military aid to Israel and has said that U.S. tax dollars should be spent domestically — on schools and healthcare in Michigan. On Monday he told ABC News, “Israel is not actually our friend.”

“He equates sending money to Israel to causing the problems here in America,” said Carey Bloom, a member of Temple Israel. “I find him to be so dangerous. The minute he was doing that, I was petrified of him, and he has never dialed back that language.”

Bloom said she has always voted for Democratic candidates and did so in the primaries but said she would vote for Rogers this year and is happily campaigning for him. 

In August, a letter from prominent Detroit-area Jews began circulating urging Jewish Democrats in the state to sign their names in support of Mike Rogers. Another letter from a group of Michigan rabbis and Jewish community leaders called “Nonnegotiable Michigan” said they will withhold support from El-Sayed if he does not change some of his positions and rhetoric on Jewish safety and Israel.

El-Sayed staff did not respond to requests for an interview.

He has been able to draw enthusiastic support from more progressive Jewish quarters.

Former U.S. Rep. Andy Levin, a Michigan native, has been working to counter the narrative from the Jewish establishment that El-Sayed is a danger to Jews.

“As a Jew who is worried about the safety of our community, Abdul is a way safer bet than Mike Rogers,” Levin said.

The Republican candidate, he points out, has had volunteer appointees to his faith coalition tied to extremist, antisemitic rhetoric, including Lorenzo Sewell, a Black evangelical pastor in Detroit who has held so-called Christian Crusader rallies that have attracted neo-Nazis. Rogers’ student outreach team includes a member who defended a leaked Young Republicans group chat filled with praise for Hitler and gas chamber jokes.

“What’s safe for the Jewish community is democracy,” Levin said. “What’s safe for the Jewish community is not authoritarianism. What’s safe for the Jewish community is minorities having representation.” 

Rogers’ campaign did not respond to an RNS request for an interview.

A host of Jewish, Muslim and Christian volunteer canvassers have been crisscrossing Detroit and its suburbs, knocking on doors on El Sayed’s behalf each weekend and sharing the message that El-Sayed will support a multiracial, multi-faith democracy. In a video posted Tuesday, the candidate says faith is a “good thing.”

Among those volunteering for him is Nusaiba Mubarak, a D.C.-based political organizer who has hired more than 20 mostly Black women from Detroit to knock on doors for El-Sayed through her group, Out Organize Strategies.

“We need Arab-American community members to learn from the Black community and the history of the Black freedom struggle,” she said.

El-Sayed has also campaigned with former Vice President Kamala Harris. Last week, U.S. Rep. Ayanna Pressley was in Detroit stumping for him. 

Venita Tompkins, who listened to El-Sayed speak at the town hall last week, walked away swayed by his willingness to bridge divides between Black and Arab Americans.

“He is being bold enough to be the catalyst, to show that healing can take place,” she said. In speaking to that issue, she said, El-Sayed had won her vote.

item.title: Catholic bishops pray over Trump days before midterms
item.dc:creator: Claire Giangravè
item.description: VATICAN CITY (RNS) — The U.S. bishops’ conference said it had no role in the Oval Office gathering, which echoed prayer sessions with Trump’s evangelical supporters.
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

VATICAN CITY (RNS) — With surveys showing declining support among Catholics for President Donald Trump and Republicans as a whole, 12 Catholic bishops offered the president an image of support this week.

On Oct. 22, twelve days before the midterms, several Catholic bishops prayed over Trump, extending their hands on him as he bowed his head in the Oval Office.

Archbishop James Golka, who was tapped by Pope Leo XIV to lead the Archdiocese of Denver in February, led the prayer thanking God for the nation, the government and the presidency.

“We lift up our president and ask your blessing upon him,” Golka said as the bishops laid hands on Trump, asking the Holy Spirit to “protect us against any influence of evil.”

Archbishop James R. Golka joined fellow Roman Catholic bishops in meeting with President Trump and led a prayer in the Oval Office, asking God’s blessing upon the president and our nation.

Read more: https://t.co/2KCnlwp7Sb

Video credit: Margo Martin https://t.co/BlrQDJjl4r

— Archdiocese of Denver (@ArchDenver) October 22, 2026

The gesture came at a politically sensitive moment. Historically, Catholic voters have supported Trump, selecting him on 52% of their ballots in 2016 and 55% in 2024, dipping to 49% in 2020, according to data from Pew Research.

Support among white Catholic voters has been even stronger, with about two-thirds voting for Trump in 2016 (64%), 2020 (68%) and 2024 (65%).

But a recent report from Pew found support for the president to be slipping. Half of white Catholic voters and 39% of Catholic voters overall said they planned to vote for the Republican candidate in their congressional district during the upcoming midterms. And according to PRRI’s American Values Survey, released Oct. 20, 61% of white Catholics said their opinion of Trump had changed mostly for the worse over the previous two years.

Videos of the bishops’ prayer began circulating Thursday afternoon on X, following posts by the Archdiocese of Denver and White House Communications Advisor Margo Martin. Austen Ivereigh, who wrote a biography on Pope Francis, called the event “sickening,” while Stephen Schneck, the president of Catholics for the Future, questioned whether the appearance followed the bishops’ own guidance on nonpartisanship. 

The U.S. Conference of Catholics Bishops, which has publicly opposed Trump’s governance of immigration and foreign policy issues, distanced itself from the White House meeting. “This is not something that the USCCB organized, and it’s not affiliated with the conference,” Chieko Noguchi, a USCCB spokesperson, told RNS.

Shortly before the White House meeting, the head of the USCCB, Archbishop Paul Coakley, urged Catholics to “put their faith before politics” and underlined the church’s role as a nonpartisan organization.

Golka is not known for his political leanings. He favored a pastoral approach during debates over banning Communion for pro-choice politicians and broadened outreach for migrants and the homeless in leading the historically conservative diocese of Denver. Six months ago, Golka criticized Trump’s attacks on Leo over the war in Iran as “not acceptable.”

But the Colorado Catholic Conference, which represents the state’s bishops, also co-sponsored an Oct. 3 get-out-the-vote event with CatholicVote, a conservative advocacy group that endorsed Trump in 2024.

The Denver Archdiocese defended the prayer over Trump, declaring in a statement Thursday that “praying for those in public office is a longstanding Catholic practice.”

“It is not an endorsement of any specific candidate or party,” the statement added.

The White House identified many of the bishops, representing a broad range of political leanings, who prayed over Trump. Among them were Archbishop emeritus Joseph Naumann of Kansas City and Bishop James Wall of the southwestern U.S. Diocese of Gallup, who have been prominent conservative voices condemning abortion and Communion for pro-choice politicians. Also participating were Bishop Michael Barber of Oakland, Bishop Edward Burns of Dallas and Archbishop Jeffrey Grob of Milwaukee, who have voiced their support for immigrants and refugees. Bishop Thomas Hennen, who was appointed by Pope Leo to lead the Diocese of Baker and who has supported outreach to LGBTQ Catholics, was there. Others like Golka who defy political labels, including Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines and Maronite Bishop Abdallah Elias Zaidan of Los Angeles, were there as well.

The Catholic blog The Pillar reported that the event was organized by Mario Enzler, a former Swiss Guard who works at the Heritage Foundation, the conservative think tank behind the hard-right political manifesto Project 2025. But Marguerite Bowling, Heritage’s senior communications manager for domestic policy, wrote this in an email to RNS: “Heritage didn’t organize this meeting. Mario Enzler was there, but he didn’t set anything up.” 

Also attending the event were the White House faith director, Jenny Korn, and Trump’s senior faith advisor, Paula White-Cain. Korn told EWTN that the meeting was part of the “ongoing engagement with faith leaders” and that the bishops and the president discussed “religious freedom, the role of the White House Faith Office, school choice, religious visas and life policy.” The Denver Archdiocese said family tax credits were also addressed.

Trump told reporters on Friday that it was “a great meeting” at which the bishops mostly prayed.

RELATED: Flashy AI campaign ads use religion to stir emotions and attack candidates

White was present at another controversial faith moment at the White House in July 2017, when evangelical leaders gathered around Trump to pray over him in a pose similar to the one captured on Thursday. Pentecostal pastor Rodney Howard-Browne, who was part of that gathering, told CBN that White had come up with the idea of praying over Trump.

The Vatican’s Dicastery for Bishops did not reply to RNS requests for comment in time for publication.

RELATED: Democratic candidates must be bad Christians

RNS staff writers Jack Jenkins and Bob Smietana contributed to this report.

item.title: Michigan’s US Senate race deeply divides the state’s Jews
item.dc:creator: Yonat Shimron
item.description: DETROIT (RNS) — Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate, has been a sharp Israel critic, dividing Michigan Jews.
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

DETROIT (RNS) — The man at the door welcomed the canvasser who inquired whether he was planning on voting in the midterms. He told the canvasser he was but was still unsure who he was going to vote for in the U.S. Senate race.

“What’s your main concern?” asked the canvasser, Frances Kunreuther.

“Abdul El-Sayed’s position on Israel,” said the man, who lives in the affluent, lakeside community of West Bloomfield, about 30 miles northwest of Detroit. “It’s making it really tough. I don’t like his answers about it. I’m not sure what to do, honestly.”

This doorstep exchange last Saturday (Oct. 17) is one of hundreds that have taken place as El-Sayed’s allies and supporters — Jews, Muslims and Christians who have fanned out across the Detroit-area in the last weeks of the campaign — try to convince voters, among them Jews, to vote for a Muslim Arab-American candidate.

The race points to the deep divisions among Michigan Jews over El-Sayed. The Senate candidate who has said he would vote to cut off U.S. military aid to Israel, and earlier this week said he did not consider Israel an ally, has created a rift among Jews there, one few voters wanted to talk about publicly.

It pits Jews for whom Israel is a big part of their identity against other Jews for whom it isn’t.

Kunreuther, a 73-year-old canvasser from New York City who had traveled to Detroit to knock on doors for El-Sayed as part of the Seed the Vote organization, is among the latter.

She told the man she was Jewish, too, and understood his concerns. Then she explained she was the daughter of a Holocaust survivor whose father came to America because he believed in democracy. El-Sayed, she said, would protect democracy better than his Republican challenger, Mike Rogers, an ally of President Donald Trump, whom she viewed as authoritarian.

“Trump is even more dangerous to Jews,” she said.

Kunreuther, along with several other Jewish canvassers, wore T-shirts that read “Jews for Shared Safety,” alluding to a vision of a multicultural American society in which people care for one another. She and a half dozen other Jewish canvassers traipsed across Halloween festooned yards full of ghosts, goblins and skeletons campaigning for El-Sayed.

Jewish voters have long been among the Democratic Party’s most reliable constituencies, but in this race that may be changing. Michigan has a Jewish population of about 130,000 people, or about 1.3% of the state’s 10 million residents, and most consider themselves Democrats.

But many Jews in Michigan said they would feel threatened with El-Sayed as their senator and they plan to withhold their vote for him or vote Republican. Rogers has been working hard to win the allegiance of Michigan voters. In an interview this week with JTA, he said Israel is “the best ally we have in the Middle East.” He has characterized his opponent as “anti-Jew” and a supporter of the Islamist movement, the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed has denied. Rogers’ staff did not respond to an RNS request for interview.

The Michigan Senate race is particularly tight, with surveys showing El-Sayed with a small lead (generally between 1 to 3 percentage points) across most polls. It’s a critical state for Democrats in their push to win control of the Senate.

But the Michigan Jewish establishment — rabbis and federation leaders — are mostly opposed to El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim senator in the United States if elected. Some 50 of its leaders, including many rabbis, recently formed Nonnegotiable Michigan. The petition drive demands, among other things, that Democratic candidates acknowledge “Jewish statehood in Israel is nonnegotiable.” (El-Sayed is not mentioned in the petition.)

“It’s important to me that our elected officials recognize the right of Israel to exist as a Jewish and democratic state; that they recognize Israel’s right to defend itself, and that they see how advantageous it is for us as Americans to be strategic allies with the state of Israel,” said Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield, Michigan, and one of the organizers of Nonnegotiable Michigan.

Starr is a prominent rabbi of a 1,000-family Conservative congregation about 20 miles northwest of Detroit. Last week, the synagogue was the host of a Justice Department event called the “American Tour Against Hate” that included a video address by President Donald Trump.

This week, El-Sayed reportedly sent a letter to Jewish voters saying he knows what it’s like to be discriminated against and that he was “committed to protecting all Michigan Jews against hatred and injustice.” It did not convince members of Nonnegotiable.who issued another letter saying his response was insufficient.

But several prominent Jewish political leaders have been energetically campaigning on behalf of El-Sayed. Brad Lander, the Democratic Party nominee for New York’s 10th congressional district, was in Detroit to campaign for El-Sayed last week. So was Daniel Biss, the Democratic candidate for Illinois’ 9th Congressional District and former mayor of Evanston.

A passionate group of volunteers — some from the progressive Reconstructionist synagogue Congregation T’chiyah in Ferndale, Michigan, and others from national Jewish groups such as IfNotNow and Bend the Arc, as well as several local chapters of Jewish Voice for Peace — has also been advocating on El-Sayed’s behalf.

Ronit Wagman, a 45-year-old book editor who lives in Oak Park, Michigan, also spent last weekend knocking on doors.

Wagman said her Judaism is rooted in social justice. She is a board member of Detroit Jews for Justice and is active with the Coalition for Property Tax Justice, a Black community-led organization fighting unfair tax assessments in Detroit.

She attends a Reform synagogue and has seen firsthand the Michigan Jewish community’s rift over the Senate race.

“There has been so much anti-Israel sentiment, which I think the community here has really conflated it with antisemitism,” Wagman said.

But for her, other issues were more important.

“I just feel very strongly about (El-Sayed’s) vision for taxing the billionaire class and creating more social programs for the middle class,” Wagman said. “I think he’s always trying to bring the conversation back to that: the economy, Michigan, getting money out of politics, and those things are very important to me.”

Wagman’s interests are in line with those of most American Jews, according to a poll by GBAO, a public opinion research firm that often polls U.S. Jews.  

“Jewish voters’ top priorities in this election are the cost of living and the future of democracy,” said Jim Gerstein, a principal with GBAO. “For Jewish voters, Israel is much lower on the priority list.”

Though he had no data for Michigan alone, Gerstein said he has found nationally that Jewish organizational leadership is more conservative politically, whereas most Jews lean left.

On the same day Wagman was canvassing for El-Sayed, Starr was gathering a stack of yard signs in his office that read “Hurt people help people.”

The signs are a rebuke to El-Sayed’s comment after a March attack on a Michigan synagogue, Temple Israel, by a radicalized Lebanese-born man. El-Sayed responded to the attack with the comment “hurt people hurt people,” which to many Jews seemed to justify or excuse the attacker’s actions. El-Sayed apologized for the remark. But for many, it was a turning point. One mother of a preschooler at the synagogue that was targeted announced her support for Rogers in an ad.

Starr, too, has made up his mind. “For me, once the absentee ballots came out, the High Holiday season ended, I knew it was time for me to say, the window has closed, and I cannot vote for Dr. El-Sayed. I cannot vote for other Democrats who speak or act the way he has,” he said. 

Starr did not say who he would vote for.

item.title: Reformation Sunday asks Christians a question: What is power for?
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Butler
item.description: (RNS) — As Haitian Christians lead a pilgrimage across Ohio, their witness offers a different vision of Christian power — and a reminder of what happens when churches forget whom they serve.
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

(RNS) — This week, as Protestants prepare to celebrate Reformation Sunday on Oct. 25, Haitian pastors and community members are leading a pilgrimage of more than 40 miles across Ohio to remind America of one of Christianity’s most fundamental commandments: Love your neighbor as yourself. 

Their four-day journey from Springfield to Columbus includes people subjected to electronic ankle monitoring and families living under the threat of detention and deportation. Fellow clergy and faith leaders are walking alongside them in solidarity, demanding an end to these practices and lasting protections for Haitian immigrants. 

The betrayal is especially profound. The United States granted Haitians Temporary Protected Status because conditions in their homeland made returning dangerous. Springfield welcomed thousands, and they helped revitalize its economy, filling jobs, starting businesses and strengthening local congregations. Now the Trump administration has terminated their protections, threatening to deport people to a country where rampant violence could cost them their lives. 

It is a remarkable act of faith and courage. And it raises a question Christians have faced repeatedly throughout history: When political leaders demand that we fear, exclude or turn away from our neighbors, whom will the church follow? 

Nearly 500 years ago, the Protestant Reformation — which many Protestants commemorate on the last Sunday in October — challenged the church’s entanglement with political power and its claims to unquestioned authority. Reformers insisted that Christians must continually return to the teachings of Jesus rather than simply accept the dictates of powerful institutions. 

That struggle did not end in the 16th century. 

Last month, I visited Dresden, Germany, where I spoke at the Frauenkirche, the magnificent church destroyed during World War II and rebuilt decades later as a symbol of reconciliation and peace. 

Standing there, I was reminded of a painful chapter in Protestant history. In the 1930s, as Hitler consolidated power, many German church leaders embraced nationalism and welcomed the promise of a restored Christian nation. The Nazi-aligned “German Christians” sought to bring the church into conformity with the ideology of the state. 

Others resisted. In 1934, leaders of what became known as the Confessing Church issued the Barmen Declaration, insisting that Jesus Christ, not the state or its political leaders, was the church’s ultimate authority. 

But that history is also a warning. Most German Christians did not resist Nazi rule. Even the Confessing Church largely failed to confront the persecution of Jews. Some recognized the danger of political control over the church without fully recognizing the suffering of their neighbors. 

It is possible to defend the church’s freedom while failing to defend the freedom of others. 

Standing in the Frauenkirche, I wondered what our own generation of Christians will be remembered for — and whether we will recognize the moment when faithfulness requires us to stand with those whose rights and dignity are under attack. 

That distinction is enormously salient today. 

Christian nationalism in America is not simply the belief that faith should inform public life. It is a political project that seeks to privilege a narrow and exclusionary vision of Christian identity in determining who belongs, whose rights are protected and who should govern. 

It places the nation, and the power to control it, ahead of our obligations to our neighbors and the wider human family. 

Such movements depend on more than political coercion. They must also reshape our moral imagination. First, they identify people to fear. Then they encourage us to look away from those people’s suffering. Once we accept that some neighbors are less deserving of dignity or freedom, restrictions on their rights become easier to justify. 

This is why the emerging campaign against empathy is so troubling. Influential voices on the religious and political right have begun portraying empathy as “toxic” or even “suicidal,” recasting a central Christian virtue as a dangerous weakness. 

New research from the Public Religion Research Institute reveals the depth of this divide. Only 38% of Christian nationalism adherents consider empathy a foundational moral value, compared with 94% of those who reject Christian nationalism. 

But empathy — the capacity to recognize another person’s suffering as morally significant — is essential to the kind of neighbor-love Jesus commanded. 

When Jesus was asked to identify the greatest commandment, he answered with two: Love God with all your heart, soul and mind. And love your neighbor as yourself. 

These commandments cannot be separated. We cannot claim devotion to God while turning away from the suffering of people made in God’s image. 

For the church, this is not a partisan preference. It is a theological obligation. 

That is what makes the pilgrimage in Ohio so significant. 

Haitian immigrants in Springfield have been targets of inflammatory political rhetoric. Families who came seeking safety and built lives as workers, parents, students and members of local congregations now face separation, detention and deportation. Some must wear ankle monitors as they go about their daily lives. 

Yet the story of Springfield is not only about persecution. It is also about Haitian pastors and community leaders who refuse to be silenced, and the clergy, congregations and organizers joining them in solidarity. 

RELATED: In direct appeal to Trump, Catholic bishops’ president urges end of mass deportations of Haitians

The pilgrimage makes visible something that authoritarian politics seeks to erase: our shared humanity. 

These faith leaders are not merely asking Americans to feel sympathy. They are acting on the conviction that another person’s suffering places a claim upon us. 

This is what it means for the church to be continually reformed. 

The Reformation is not simply an anniversary of an event in 1517. It is an ongoing invitation to examine where the church has confused its own security, privilege or political influence with faithfulness to Christ. 

Today, many mainline Protestant congregations are rediscovering this calling. Some are small. Some have declining memberships and uncertain futures. Yet they are feeding neighbors, accompanying immigrant families, defending religious freedom and building communities of belonging in places where fear threatens to prevail. 

I recently argued in The Hill that mainline Protestants could emerge as an important swing constituency in American politics, challenging the dominance of the white evangelical voting bloc that has helped sustain Republican power. I believe that still. Our congregations have far more moral authority, community reach and political potential than the familiar narrative of mainline decline suggests. 

But Reformation Sunday reminds us that the question is not simply whether we can reclaim power. It is what kind of power we seek and to what end.

Christian nationalism seeks power over others — the power to determine who belongs, whose rights deserve protection and whose religious beliefs should shape the nation’s laws. 

The power of a reformed church must look different. It is the power to speak truth to those who govern, defend the dignity of the vulnerable and build communities where people can live together across differences. 

That kind of influence is not politically insignificant. It can change public policy, elections and the direction of our democracy. But it begins with a different understanding of what it means to be faithful. 

Reformation Sunday invites us to celebrate the courage of those who challenged the religious authorities of their time. It should also invite us to examine our own. 

The Haitian pastors leading the pilgrimage across Ohio are showing us what faithful public witness looks like. They are not seeking power over others. They are demanding that their neighbors be treated with dignity and inviting the rest of us to stand alongside them. 

Perhaps the most important test of a church that claims to be continually reformed is not how much power it can accumulate but how it uses its influence when its neighbors are in danger. 

(The Rev. Jennifer Butler is a Presbyterian minister, pastor of Rockville Presbyterian Church in Maryland and founder of Faith in Democracy. She is the author of “Born Again: The Christian Right Globalized and Who Stole My Bible? Reclaiming Scripture as a Handbook for Resisting Tyranny.” The views expressed in this commentary do not necessarily reflect those of Religion News Service.)

 

RELATED: As Springfield prepares to bury Haitian student, sympathy surges and deportations continue

item.title: Indian Gen Z ‘cockroach’ protesters aim to upend assumptions about democracy – and populism – in Modi’s India
item.dc:creator: Susanna Granieri
item.description: (The Conversation) — The protests challenge the government’s view of who “the people” are, what democracy means, and who speaks for youth, women and the politically marginalized.
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

(The Conversation) — Five months after its founding, India’s Cockroach Janta Party, known as the CJP, has revealed what youth-led democratic movements can achieve – and how hard they are to sustain.

The movement was formed in May 2026 to protest the government’s cancellation of medical school entrance exams and after India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant likened unemployed youth to cockroaches. By July, the largely Gen Z movement had scored an early victory with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The CJP has since moved on to a much larger political issue: The Election Commission’s reported deletion of approximately 130 million names from the voter rolls. Since Oct. 2, protesters have descended on the streets of Delhi, Mumbai and other cities demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, halting the deletions pending an independent inquiry, and the restoration of the old electoral rolls before the next elections.

In the process, the CJP has encountered strong government resistance.. Amid a crackdown on protests, two of the movement’s spokespersons – Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das – were detained, while Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his right-wing populist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, have refused to bend on the voter roll issue – instead accusing protesters of undermining democracy.

Nonetheless, as a long-time scholar of Indian political parties and social movements, I believe the CJP’s protests have revealed people’s deep-seated anxieties over democratic erosion in a country of nearly 1.5 billion. Through courage and acerbic wit, the CJP has done something that has eluded conventional opposition parties over the past 12 years: puncturing the ruling party’s aura of invulnerability. In doing so, I believe the protests have challenged the government’s view of who “the people” are, what democracy means, and who speaks for youth, women and the politically marginalized.

Defining ‘democracy’ and ‘the people’

Modi often describes India as the “Mother of Democracy,” a reference to its civilizational heritage and to Bharat Mata, the Hindu mother goddess. Democracy, he insists, is not a Western import but a native inheritance. The implication is meant to be reassuring: India has always been democratic and always will be.

Workers and activists of various opposition parties march toward the Supreme Court demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi on Oct. 12, 2026.
AP Photo/Manish Swarup

But some outside monitors disagree. Sweden’s V-Dem Institute classifies India as an “electoral autocracy,” meaning that although it regularly holds multiparty elections, it fails basic democratic benchmarks such as legislative and judicial checks and balances and citizens’ active political participation.

Judged by how the country treats dissent, the record is damning: using anti-terrorism laws to jail activists without trial, barricading protest sites, internet blackouts and police brutality.

By contrast, the CJP considers peaceful protest, along with upholding the country’s constitution, essential elements of democracy. Demonstrators regularly circulate images of B. R. Ambedkar – the chief architect of the Indian constitution – on posters, in slogans and in songs. Like Ambedkar, 30-year-old CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke is a Dalit, or untouchable within the Hindu caste system.

Critics argue that the BJP defines the nation through Hindu civilizational identity, which is exclusionary because it rejects India’s rich Muslim historical traditions and casts doubt on the political loyalties of the country’s Muslims, who constitute about 14% of the population – 197 million people. By contrast, the CJP draws no line between insider and outsider by faith, caste or birth, and it defines community by shared commitments.

The voter roll struggle shows what is at stake in the question. The Election Commission says the revision will remove duplicate entries, deceased voters and noncitizens. But critics worry that the burden of proof falls on voters. Consider how hard it is for poor Muslims, Dalits and migrant workers to produce decades-old birth, education and land certificates. Moreover, those whose names are struck from the electoral rolls fear being branded illegal immigrants.

Cracks appear in BJP’s dominance

While the BJP had held the prime minister’s office before, Modi’s 2014 election marked a sea change in Indian politics, disrupting the Congress Party’s dominance.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrives at the presidential palace in New Delhi, India, on Oct. 5, 2026.
AP Photo/Manish Swarup

The BJP owed it electoral success in part to attracting young and first-time voters with promises of employment, economic growth and what is known in Hindi as “achhe din aane waale hain,” or “good days are coming.” Since the BJP took office in 2014, the country has charted strong GDP growth, but the macroeconomic success has been belied by ongoing and rampant inequality that falls especially hard on the poor and young.

The BJP claims to have fulfilled some of its more targeted campaign promises, such as engaging in merit-based public sector hiring. Yet 40% of Indian college graduates under 25 are unemployed. Paradoxically, the unemployment rate for youth who cannot read and write hovers around just 3.4%. For college graduates, who are the CJP’s main constituency, it is nearly nine times higher at roughly 29%.

Seizing on this building discontent, the CJP uses the slogan “Achhe Din” ironically, on posters and memes. Its manifesto opens: “If you are going to call us cockroaches, the least you can do is pay our rent.” It calls for making “lazy” – a code word for the unemployed – a protected political identity.

Underlying the joke is a serious point: that stigmatization of the jobless offends millions of impoverished people, something critics note is protected in the dignity and equality guarantees of articles 21 and 14 of the Constitution.

Who speaks for women?

The BJP has gained women’s electoral support through a combination of targeted welfare schemes, support for increased women’s representation in legislatures and endless talk of women’s empowerment, or “nari shakti.”

However, masses of women protesters have challenged state-defined women’s empowerment. They stop police vans carrying detainees, scale barricades and criticize the prime minister.

One of the most prominent among them is Neha Bora, a Ph.D. student and president of the left-wing All India Students’ Association, whose blunt messages to Modi has seen her profile skyrocket. Modi has said he has been subject to vulgar abuses by the protesters and was shocked by how “our daughters” could use such foul language, but he viewed them as “misdirected children” and was ready to forgive them.

The throngs of women who are protesting express deep discontent with the government’s paternalism. They challenge its Hindu-inflected understanding of empowerment and insist on speaking for themselves rather than being spoken for. They express outrage at the government’s brutal response to their peaceful protests. They describe how the police have beaten and sexually harassed them, while anonymous self-styled guardians of religious morality engage in doxing, threats of rape and acid attacks, and circulate demeaning AI-generated images of them. For protesters, that record sits uneasily besides the prime minister’s denunciation of violence against women.

‘Cockroaches never die’

The CJP motto, “Cockroaches never die,” has wide resonance. Protesters have survived, but not escaped, violence, incarceration, internet blackouts and police blockades. The sunglass-wearing cockroach mascot makes a mockery of leader-centered nationalist branding.

CJP supporters take part in a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in Mumbai, India, on Oct. 2, 2026.
AP Photo/Rafiq Maqbool

Recent youth-led uprisings in Bangladesh and Nepal have shown how quickly online mobilization can outrun official control. What distinguishes the CJP is that it pairs humor with legal and technical infrastructure. Its online portal Saakshi vault, which means “witness,” collects photos and videos of police violence that protesters upload; volunteer lawyers use these to issue complaints against officers.

The CJP’s recent and remarkable successes do not mean that the movement is likely to disrupt the BJP’s hold on power in the next parliamentary elections in 2029. For now at least, the CJP is fairly concentrated in urban strongholds and would need to build organizational infrastructure and develop long-term demands.

However, a generation that a government minister wrote off as lazy and expendable has exposed the cracks in the system that the chief justice defended. Whatever form it takes, the movement provides a vision and reminder of what democracy looks like.

(Amrita Basu, Professor of Political Science, and Sexuality, Women’s and Gender Studies, Amherst College. The views expressed in this commentary do not necessarily reflect those of Religion News Service.)

item.title: The key message of the LDS Church’s new Visitors’ Center? We’re Christian, darn it.
item.dc:creator: Jana Riess
item.description: (RNS) — If the church’s new Visitors’ Center is a preview of next year’s Temple Square celebration, the message will be all about Jesus.
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

(RNS) — A few months ago, I had the opportunity to take a special tour of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints’ new Visitors’ Center on Temple Square in Salt Lake City. It felt great to be back on Temple Square for the first time in years. The area has been mostly closed while the church has undertaken extensive renovations to the Salt Lake Temple, which is scheduled to reopen in 2027.

Before it reopens for church members to perform sacred ordinances, the temple will open to the public. It’s standard procedure in Mormonism to let non-members tour new temples for a few weeks before they’re dedicated because afterward, they aren’t permitted inside. But the newly renovated Salt Lake Temple is going to be open for six full months of public tours, from April to October 2027. (Make your reservations now. The tickets are free, but they need to be requested in advance.)

In addition to the coming temple tours, the church is also reaching out to outsiders via the brand-new Visitors’ Center tour I took in June. These tours, according to the church’s website, aim to “explore the purpose of temples on a guided tour that reveals its sacred spaces.”

RELATED: Do Mormons worship Jesus Christ?

I had two main takeaways from my time in the Visitors’ Center, both largely positive.

First, there’s a noticeable emphasis on Christianity. There’s almost nothing in the displays about founding prophet Joseph Smith or Mormon pioneers in prairie clothes. Instead, art depicting Jesus fills the space, with the Christus statue taking pride of place.

All over the Visitors’ Center, the art showcases Jesus Christ as the center of the LDS faith. The message is very clear that we — and I say we because I’m also a member — are Christians. The carefully planned Visitors’ Center experience strikes me as an overt declaration of that Christian identity, especially in an era when many evangelical Protestants continue to doubt that Latter-day Saints are real followers of Jesus.

Their challenges aren’t just theoretical, either. In June, the U.S. Department of Defense, led by conservative evangelical Pete Hegseth, initially omitted the LDS Church from the government’s official list of Christian denominations. After facing backlash from Utah’s congressional contingent and many other critics, the department later reversed course. Still, for Latter-day Saints, the initial false classification stung.

The art in and outside the Visitors’ Center was created long before the Department of Defense debacle. But it seems to have anticipated exactly those kinds of objections to LDS Christianity, and takes pains to emphasize over and over: “We’re Christian, darn it!” (Insert stronger language than “darn” if the Spirit so moves.)  

The art moves the LDS Church closer to traditional Protestant and Catholic artistic and theological traditions. One big surprise for longtime Latter-day Saints is the beautiful sculpture of Christ carrying his cross.

RELATED: The Mormon Jesus

That’s a different look for the LDS Church. In the past, church presidents have discouraged members from wearing crosses or using crosses as decoration because the focus of the LDS Church was the risen Lord rather than Christ and his suffering. This is an interesting departure.

My second takeaway is that the new Visitors’ Center goes further than the church ever has in demystifying the temple. When you come inside, you walk through replicas of the main rooms inside the temple that you would experience if you’re a Latter-day Saint going there to do sacred ordinances.

You’ll see copies of the rooms where church members can do baptisms for the dead or get married for all eternity. And while you’re there, a trained guide — mine was a recently returned missionary — can answer questions.

The Visitors’ Center experience is not just about demystifying the temple for outsiders, but for members themselves. I was interested to see that a cutaway model shows parts of the Salt Lake Temple most members never see, including the upper room where the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles meets weekly.

The church is planning for millions to visit Temple Square in 2027. And if the center is a preview, the message will be all about Jesus.

RELATED: On 30 years of Mormon belonging and not-belonging

item.title: Multisite churches — also known as franchises — are now a staple of American life
item.dc:creator: Ron Ribiat
item.description: (RNS) — A new study of multi-site churches has found that such congregations have become commonplace, found in almost every state in the nation. Many of the 1,800 multisite churches have started a new location by merging with another church.
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

(RNS) — At least 5 million Americans attend a multisite church, where they often watch a video beamed in from another site and have access to all the advantages of a megachurch without the crowds.

The multisite movement, which started with a handful of large churches in the 1990s, is now relatively commonplace. An estimated 1,800 churches use that model nationwide, according to “Multisite Revealed,” a new report from The Ascent Leader, an evangelical leadership training group.

All told, those churches have about 6,000 local sites, known as campuses. And they are found in almost every state in the union.

“Where are multisite churches located?” Warren Bird, the lead researcher on the report, said during an online event Wednesday (Oct. 21) highlighting the report. “Everywhere but Wyoming.”

RELATED: Andy Stanley, pastor of North Point Church, to resign in 2027

 The report, which drew on survey responses from more than 1,000 church leaders, found that more than half (57%) of multisite churches, which are predominantly evangelical, are found in suburban settings. A quarter are in rural settings, while 18% are in urban areas.

Most of the country’s largest Protestant churches are multisite, including almost all those on the list of the top 25 largest congregations compiled by Outreach Magazine. The lone exception in that group is Lakewood Church, led by televangelist and author Joel Osteen, which meets in a former basketball arena in downtown Houston. (Resurrection United Methodist Church in Kansas, led by pastor and U.S. Senate candidate Adam Hamilton, ranks No. 89 on the Outreach list with just under 10,000 attendees and has six locations.)

To qualify for the survey, churches had to meet in more than one location while sharing the same budget and leadership. Churches in the survey had an average of 3.4 campuses, and those campuses had a median attendance of 395 people. That makes those campuses larger than the median-sized U.S. church, which draws about 70 people to worship.

About half of the churches (52%) had two or three campuses. A few (3%) had 10 or more.

Bird said that churches in the survey aren’t all the same. About 4 in 10 are franchises, where every service is nearly identical and all decisions are made from the central office. A similar number use what researchers called a “federation model,” which all have the same branding and are led from a central office but aren’t identical. The rest have a “family model” with shared leaders but some local differences.

Researchers found that campuses for multisite churches are growing by about 9% each year, with faster growth (16%) happening in the first five years of a church’s existence. 

“This research shows us that multisite has proven to be an effective and adaptable church reproduction model,” said author and consultant Jim Tomberlin, who co-authored the report.

One of the most contested topics among multisite churches is whether they stream the sermon by video from a central location or have a live preacher in the building. Bird said researchers wanted to know if using video preaching, which is common in the largest multisite churches, remains commonplace.

They found that about one in four (27%) multisite churches never use video preaching. Another 18% use it less than 10 times a year. About half of churches use video at least 25 weekends or more a year.

“Churches with just two campuses, which is half of all multisite churches, use little video teaching,” Bird said.

Almost all multisite churches (92%) use a team of preachers. 

Among the biggest challenges for multisite churches is finding enough leaders and facilities for their campuses.

“What’s the most named challenge or obstacle in launching a new campus? In a word — it’s locating a suitable facility,” said Tomberlin. “Close behind is a leadership shortage.”

Between 30% and 40% of facilities were acquired in mergers between a larger church and a smaller church.

“Our survey findings underscored the reality that mergers are a prominent vehicle of multisite churches for campus expansion and for church revitalization,” Bird said.

 A new campus costs about $1,250 per worshiper to start up, according to the report. Just over half become self-sufficient within three years.

About half the churches in the survey had started a new campus within the past three years. And researchers expect that trend to continue.

“The multisite movement is developing some serious wings,” Bird said.

RELATED: Turnaround: How dying churches can find new life

item.title: New Vatican document cautions against ‘triumphalism’ over rise in baptisms
item.dc:creator: Claire Giangravè
item.category: Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith
item.description: VATICAN CITY (RNS) — A new Vatican document welcomes rising baptisms as signs of hope but warns against triumphalism, urging Catholic communities to help converts build lasting faith.
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

VATICAN CITY (RNS) – As countries including the United States and France report a rise in the number of young Catholic converts, a new Vatican document cautions against triumphalism, arguing that new baptisms don’t always lead to lasting religious commitment.

The document, titled “Venite ad Me (Come to Me): Considerations on the Transmission of the Faith in an Epochal Change,” was released Thursday (Oct. 22). It addresses the struggles, challenges and opportunities of the Catholic Church and its families in passing the faith to new generations. Issued by the Vatican Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, it reflects on how social media and secularization are coloring how young people approach their beliefs.

In a section titled “New Frontiers of Evangelization,” the document remarks on “the growing number of conversions and returns to the Church, especially among youth and young adults,” in secularized areas of Europe and America. Citing data from the French bishops’ conference, the document reported that France saw a 26% increase in baptisms in 2026 over the previous year.

The vast majority, the document reads, are younger than 40 and seek the Catholic faith after a time of crisis, spiritual awakening or contact with other believers.

“A broader view of the situation, however, suggests adopting a cautious approach when evaluating this reality,” the document reads, adding that the growth in baptisms has coincided with the parallel challenge of making sure the newly baptized maintain their faith.

“While it is appropriate to avoid triumphalistic attitudes in this regard, it cannot be denied that these phenomena constitute concrete signs of hope and evangelical vitality,” it added. The document also suggested a need to promote community and welcome new members into the church.

The Vatican document comes shortly after Pope Leo XIV convened a summit of heads of bishops’ conferences and experts to the Vatican for the 10th anniversary of Pope Francis’ apostolic exhortation “Amoris Laetitia (The Joy of Love).” The conference, held Oct. 7-24, discussed among other things the struggles of families in transmitting the faith and how the church can accompany parents in this effort.

A final document will be published in the coming weeks, once it has been approved by the pope.

Its reporting on the rise of adult conversions in parts of Western Europe is particularly poignant since Leo visited France Sep. 25-28. There, he was welcomed by large crowds of catechumens and newly baptized Catholics in Paris and attended a vigil with more than 80,000 young people. Recalling the event, Leo labeled the Catholic renewal in France “a great sign of hope.”

RELATED: El-Sayed, Vance pressed on religion, loyalty and immigration

The Vatican document reflects the cautions of Paris-area bishops, who called for a year-long provincial ecclesial assembly in May to address the boom in baptisms. Speaking to RNS before the papal trip, Bishop Matthieu Rougé of Nanterre, who chairs the French bishops’ council for Catholic education, cautioned that the influx of converts “remains limited and fragile, and should not give rise to any pride or misplaced triumphalism.”

The document also highlights the “appeal that both traditional and more recent forms of pilgrimage hold for the younger generations” as well as the importance for the church to showcase how the variety of its liturgy enables outreach to “different sensibilities.” In France, the Chartres Pentecost pilgrimage, organized by Notre-Dame de Chrétienté and strongly associated with the traditional Latin Mass, drew 20,000 pilgrims this year with an average age of 22, organizers said.

The document, divided into eight chapters, also calls for greater participation of women in church leadership roles. And alongside its emphasis on belonging and personal encounters, it warns that digital evangelization can become detached from daily life or shaped by ideology and personal preferences.

RELATED: Pope Leo is teaching the church the virtue of patience

item.title: FrontGate Media announces sponsorship and advertising representation for Faith On Film TV
item.dc:creator: RNS Press Release Distribution Service
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

New relationship connects advertisers and sponsors with Christian entertainment audiences through trusted industry voices and compelling faith-and-family storytelling.

ORANGE COUNTY, Calif. — FrontGate Media today announced a new representation relationship with Faith On Film TV, providing advertisers and sponsors access to a Christian entertainment program featuring the creators, stories, and conversations shaping faith-and-family media.

As FrontGate Media celebrates its 25th anniversary, the partnership reinforces the agency’s commitment to connecting brands with Christian and family audiences through trusted voices and content-driven opportunities.

Hosted by Isaac Hernandez and Holly McClure, Faith On Film TV features interviews with actors, producers, directors, writers, and creative leaders in Christian entertainment. The program introduces viewers to faith-based films and shows that entertain, educate, inspire, and share meaningful messages.

“Faith On Film is a natural fit for FrontGate because it sits at the intersection of faith, family, entertainment, and trusted storytelling,” said Scott A. Shuford, Founder & Chief Engagement Officer of FrontGate Media. “For 25 years, we’ve helped brands connect authentically with Christian audiences. This partnership gives advertisers access to a highly relevant environment where viewers are already engaged with the stories and creators shaping faith-based entertainment.”

Hernandez brings more than four decades of Christian entertainment experience, including producing and directing hundreds of television programs for Trinity Broadcasting Network, helping launch Parables TV, and executive producing independent faith-based films. He also produces and directs the ICVM Crown Awards, launched Faith On Film in 2019, and continues to consult with streaming companies, distributors, and producers.

McClure brings decades of experience as a producer, creative director, writer, film critic, and media professional. Her work includes marketing and promotional production for The Passion of the Christ, along with numerous Christian film and television projects. She currently serves as PR & Media Director for Capernaum Studios.

Together, the hosts combine entertainment expertise, industry relationships, and faith-market insight, creating a valuable platform for sponsors seeking to reach audiences interested in Christian films, family entertainment, streaming content, books, ministry, and values-driven culture.

“Marketers want more than impressions. They want credibility, audience alignment, and trusted voices,” Shuford added. “Faith On Film provides that connection through meaningful conversations with the people shaping Christian entertainment.”

For advertising and sponsorship opportunities with Faith On Film TV, or to explore FrontGate Media’s Christian and family audience solutions, visit www.FrontGateMedia.com.

About Faith On Film TV

Faith On Film TV is a faith-and-family entertainment program hosted by Isaac Hernandez and Holly McClure. Featuring interviews with actors, filmmakers, and entertainment industry professionals, the show introduces audiences to independent Christian entertainment and the creators behind stories that inspire faith, family values, and meaningful conversations. Visit www.FaithOnFilmTV.com.

About FrontGate Media

FrontGate Media is an award-winning, full-service marketing agency and media group specializing in the Faith and Family audience. With over 7,500 campaigns and a powerful digital network, FrontGate provides public relations, advertising, media buying, social marketing, and content development services. Its work has earned recognition from the Internet Advertising Competition, the WebAwards, and the Emmy® Awards. Visit www.FrontGateMedia.com.

item.title: Flashy AI campaign ads use religion to stir emotions and attack candidates
item.dc:creator: Fiona André
item.description: (RNS) — In some key races, AI has been used in campaign ads to depict candidates’ religious views and convey religious messaging, ranging from highly realistic to provocative and eccentric.
item.content:encoded:
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!

(RNS) — In a recent campaign ad for Ken Paxton, the Trump-endorsed Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate in Texas, his Democratic opponent James Talarico appears to sit at a desk while he scribbles on a Bible page.

“I always think of myself as a Christian who hates Christianity,” says the ad’s Talarico before adding that God was a “radical feminist” who “never asked people to worship him,” a reference to Talarico’s liberal Christian views, which have drawn criticism from political opponents.

The scene seems realistic and pulls quotes from Talarico’s speeches and his sermons at his Presbyterian church. Yet, it is not an actual clip of Talarico. It was created with artificial intelligence.

The 30-second clip, which has 2.6 million views on X since its release in September, is part of a flurry of AI-generated political ads airing on cable, streaming and digital platforms across the country ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. As AI content spreads online, political strategists have used the technology to create glossy campaign videos. According to a Wesleyan Media Project report released in September, 164 ads generated or enhanced by AI have been released this election cycle, costing $80 million.

In some key races, AI has been used to depict candidates’ religious views and convey religious messaging through campaign ads ranging from highly realistic to provocative and eccentric.

RELATED: El-Sayed, Vance pressed on religion, loyalty and immigration

Layering catchy music, colorful images and provocative captions, the AI campaign ads can elicit strong emotional reactions, said Heidi Campbell, author of “Digital Creatives and the Rethinking of Religious Authority” and a communication professor at Texas A&M University.

“Political ads have always tried to get you to respond out of your gut to either like or not like a person,” she said, adding strategists now “use the features of AI to kind of get people to bypass thinking and focus on emotion.”

A spokesperson for Talarico’s campaign told RNS that the Paxton campaign resorted to AI deepfake videos to manipulate Texas voters. “Dark money groups are lying about James Talarico because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.

Talarico also reacted to the ad in an interview with CNN, saying Texans were “sick of these AI ads trying to deceive voters, putting words in my mouth.”

The Paxton campaign did not respond to an RNS request for comment.

An AI ad created by The Front Line Action, a super PAC that describes itself as “countering right-wing antisemitism” and supported by Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, focuses on Michigan Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed’s Muslim faith. An AI depiction of El-Sayed is seen successively posing with four Muslim women wearing niqab, or a face veil, and stomping on an Israeli flag. In one shot, he cheers with an AI depiction of his sister and of left-wing streamer Hasan Piker in a living room as they read old tweets written on flash cards.

“The destruction of Israel and the West isn’t just a game for them, it’s a mission,” says a narrator, before adding, “His sister hates everything about America, his pal Hasan Piker thinks America deserved 9/11 and his father-in-law founded a charity tied to the Muslim Brotherhood.”

The video’s claims refer to comments Piker made in 2019 during a Twitch livestream. El-Sayed has been asked to distance himself from the streamer over those comments; he later said he disagreed with Piker on “many, many things” but refused to disavow him. The video also alludes to El-Sayed’s father-in-law, Tayeb Jukaku, who sat on the boards of two Islamic organizations named as unindicted co-conspirators in the 2008 criminal trial of the Holy Land Foundation, a defunct Muslim charity accused of sending money to Hamas-run groups in Gaza.

Attacks on candidates’ religious views or identity are a decades-old political strategy, said Isaac Sharp, a program manager at the Princeton Theological Seminary who specializes in religion and the ethical implications of AI. Recalling Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign controversy related to comments made by his spiritual adviser, the Rev. Jeremiah A. Wright, about America, he added that AI is taking this tactic to another level.

RELATED: Charlie Kirk’s AI resurrection ushers in a new era of digital grief

“It seems with these videos, it’s possible to take a group of statements that somebody has made, pull them totally out of context, and almost instantly reconfigure them in a sleek production that can paint basically any picture that they want,” he said. “That is a new frontier.”

Campbell also explained the appeal of AI tools for producing campaign ads due to their efficiency in creating original content quickly, with minimal effort and fewer resources.

“It’s faster. You can do a lot more creative things,” she said. “It’s much more economical, and you can just do it in a much more very emotional, very attention-grabbing kind of way.”

In North Carolina, Republican state senate candidate Michael Lee ran an AI ad showing his Democratic challenger, Jessica Bichler, a yoga teacher, leading a practice in a brightly-lit studio. The background shows Buddha sculptures with Bichler’s campaign pins. “You guessed it! AI was definitely used to generate these silly video clips,” read the video captions as an AI effect morphs Bichler’s legs into noodle limbs.

The Wesleyan Media Project found most of the AI ads (80%) were paid for by conservative and Republican groups, and 11% were run by liberal and Democratic sponsors. The project told RNS it had not tracked how many AI-generated campaign ads mentioned religion.

In one ad, liked nearly 15,000 times on Facebook and promoting Greg Dolezal, a Republican Georgia state senator running for lieutenant governor, AI clips of schoolgirls wearing hijabs are followed by depictions of terrorists breaking into houses. Characters dressed in Pashtun clothing, worn by the Taliban in Afghanistan, bar a woman from driving and patrol a suburban Georgia street. The caption “Keep Georgia Sharia Free” shows up on screen at the end. The video doesn’t disclose the use of AI.

In fact, most ads (69%) reviewed by the Wesleyan Media Project didn’t disclose the use of AI tools. Only 31 states have laws regulating the use of AI-generated content in political advertising, usually referred to as “deepfakes,” “synthetic media” or “deceptive media” in bills, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. California, Minnesota and Texas prohibit the publication of deepfakes of candidates in the lead-up to an election altogether. 

The videos, which embed information and images, also raise fact-checking concerns, Sharp said.

“It’s always also been a challenge of distinguishing truth from unreality or fiction,” he said. “I don’t know if a fact checking expose would even be a helpful strategy in trying to contain it.”
